newsitem.title: EGYPT: Palestinians, Israelis differ over tourism.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians, Israelis differ over tourism.

text.p: Palestinians accused Israel on Wednesday of destroying its tourism industry but an Israeli official said its policy was driven by the need to ensure the security of the Jewish state.
Mohammed Shtayeh of the Palestinian Authority said Israel's closure of the self-rule areas ruined tourism prospects and called on the Jewish state to implement its peace pledges.

"The closure has done severe damage to our tourism...there is a direct linkage between progress on the peace track and progress on tourism and economic cooperation," he told a session at the Middle East and North Africa Economic Conference.
"How can we talk about travel plans through the region when the Palestinians cannot get from Bethlehem to Jerusalem?"
Israel restricted the transport of goods and people from the self-rule areas after suicide bombings by Moslem militants killed 59 people in February and March. It has since eased some measures.

Mordechai Benari, director of international relations at the Israeli Ministry of Tourism, told reporters peace would expand his people's travel plans but that could only be achieved after the Jewish state's security concerns were satisfied.
Benari told Reuters Arab restrictions made Israelis "the most discriminated against tourists" in the region but that peace would not solve the problem.

"We can't go to Lebanon or Syria and the Gulf because of the slow peace process," he said. "But do you think that with a peace treaty signed and lots of kisses flying around, the security problems will disappear?"
"We don't do closures because we are evil. We're protecting ourselves. We might have peace by the end of the decade but security problems will last longer than that," he added.
Israel's peace talks with Syria and Lebanon have been deadlocked for years over the withdrawal of the Jewish state from lands it occupied in a 1967 war.

The right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejects the land-for-peace principle his predecessor accepted. He is also trying to renegotiate an agreed troop redeployment from the occupied West Bank town of Hebron for security reasons.
